analysis.one_liner: Lets private employers give workers paid time off instead of cash overtime pay.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in January 2020 and referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, where it sat with no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal overtime law so a private employer could offer an hourly worker 1.5 hours of paid time off instead of the 1.5 hours of cash overtime pay the worker is legally owed. Workers would have to agree in writing, couldn't be forced, could carry up to 160 hours of banked time, and could cash out on request. The bill included anti-coercion rules, employer liability for violations, required government reports, and expired after five years. It never got a committee hearing or a vote in either chamber.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers gain the most concrete benefit: overtime they would owe in cash can instead be booked as time off, so the money stays on the employer's books until the worker uses the time, asks for it, leaves, or the year ends. Some workers with predictable schedules and a real desire for time off — for family, school, or caregiving — could genuinely benefit from having the choice. But the financial flexibility flows to the employer, not the worker: the worker is owed time rather than money.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers of hourly workers; some workers wanting time off

how_it_helps.text: Lets an employee choose paid time off at 1.5 hours per overtime hour worked, in lieu of cash overtime pay, with a written voluntary agreement that is not a condition of employment and only after 1,000 hours with that employer.

Bars employers from intimidating, threatening, or coercing workers over requesting or refusing compensatory time, or from forcing workers to use it, and makes violators liable to the employee for damages plus an equal amount in liquidated damages.

Protects the worker's payout: unused time must be paid in cash by January 31 each year, in excess of 80 hours on 30 days notice, on a written request within 30 days, and at termination — at whichever is higher, the wage rate when the time was earned or when it is paid.
Includes oversight and limits: GAO reports for four years on employer use, employee uptake, and complaints, and the whole act sunsets after five years.

analysis.who_pays: Hourly workers who rely on overtime cash to make ends meet. Under the bill, money they earned at a premium rate becomes time off the employer controls the timing of — the employer can refuse a request to use the time if it would 'unduly disrupt' operations — and the employer holds the cash until it is used, requested, or paid out. The safeguards are only as strong as the worker's willingness to file a complaint against their own boss.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hourly workers who need overtime cash now

drawbacks.text: It converts a cash obligation into a deferred one: an employer can owe a worker 1.5 hours of time off instead of 1.5 hours of pay, and the employer keeps the money in the meantime — an interest-free delay of wages the worker has already earned, which hits hardest at low wages.

An employer can deny a worker's request to actually use the accrued time if the employer decides it would unduly disrupt operations, so the 'flexibility' can exist on paper while the worker keeps working the overtime.

The anti-coercion rules depend on enforcement: a worker who feels pressured to accept time off instead of pay must prove intimidation or coercion to recover, and the bill provides no new funding for Labor Department enforcement.

For employees not covered by a union contract, the agreement can be made individually before the work is performed, which puts the bargaining over pay-versus-time between one worker and their employer.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is genuinely drafted with worker protections — voluntary written agreement, a higher-of pay rate on cash-out, annual payout, damages for coercion — and some workers would welcome the option. But the core trade it offers is a bad one for the workers least able to make it: trading money already earned for time the employer controls, at no interest, with enforcement left to individual complaints. Workers with bargaining power and stable schedules could come out fine; the typical hourly worker who counts on overtime cash would not.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee in January 2020 and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote in either chamber before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Martha Roby introduced the bill on January 17, 2020, with 15 other Republican members joining at introduction.
Sixteen Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did.

The House action history shows only two steps — introduction and referral to the Committee on Education and Labor — with no committee vote, no report, and no floor action through the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021.
Under the bill's own terms it would have expired five years after enactment and required annual GAO reports on how often employers and workers used the option.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hourly workers are no worse off: the current rule that overtime must be paid in cash remains. Employers who wanted the ability to substitute time off for overtime pay gained nothing from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hourly workers keep cash overtime; employers gain nothing

sides.party_line_note: All 17 original sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic cosponsors, and the Democratic-majority Education and Labor Committee never took the bill up.

industries.industry: Private employers of hourly workers (retail, food service, manufacturing, healthcare)
industries.note: The bill would let them satisfy the overtime-pay requirement with time off instead of cash, keeping the money on their books until it is used, requested, or paid out — a cash-flow benefit paid for by workers' pay timing. The bill's own safeguards (voluntary agreement, cash-out rights, damages) are designed to police how employers use this power.

For union-represented employees, compensatory time could only be provided under the terms of a collective bargaining agreement, leaving unions in control; but unions generally opposed the bill as an erosion of the cash-overtime guarantee for nonunion workers.
